Mejuri rewrote jewelry retail by launching the weekly "Monday Drop" in 2015, treating fine jewelry like fashion and making pieces women buy for themselves-no waiting for gifts. Founded in Toronto, the brand stripped away luxury's gatekeeping and steep markups to offer accessible, everyday fine jewelry. Its direct-to-consumer model and hybrid retail footprint fueled rapid global growth and strong engagement. From a family-rooted startup to a global DTC leader, Mejuri's playbook blends fast product cadence, community-driven storytelling, and physical stores to scale; explore its strategic blueprint in the Mejuri Canvas Business Model. Compare its trajectory with peers like Quince and Kendra Scott to see how introductions-functional context-setting components-differentiate brand positioning, value proposition, and audience mapping. What is the Mejuri Founding Story? Mejuri was officially launched in 2015 by Noura Sakkijha, a third‑generation jeweler, together with her husband Majed Masad. With an MBA and a background in industrial engineering, Sakkijha spotted a structural gap: fine jewelry was largely marketed toward men buying for women. Drawing on her family's jewelry roots in Jordan and a modern, data‑driven approach to manufacturing and supply chain, the founders positioned Mejuri to empower women to buy jewelry for themselves. Built as a lean direct‑to‑consumer brand, Mejuri bypassed traditional wholesalers and high‑street markups to offer "affordable luxury." The company launched with a minimum viable product of minimalist 14k gold rings and earrings using ethically sourced gemstones, pivoting early from a crowdsourced design model to an in‑house design team to protect quality and brand identity. Bootstrapped initially and later supported by a seed round including backers like BDC Capital, Mejuri tackled the trust barrier of online fine‑jewelry purchases and scaled quickly-reaching tens of millions in revenue within its first five years by focusing on repeat customers and high gross margins typical of direct‑to‑consumer jewelry brands. Early Growth and Expansion of Mejuri saw the brand move quickly from digital-only roots to an omnichannel jeweler, fueled by major venture capital and a data-driven product cadence. After a seed round, Mejuri closed a $5M Series A in 2018 and a $23M Series B in 2019 led by Imaginary Ventures, enabling headcount growth from ~20 to over 100 within 18 months and a move to a larger Toronto headquarters. The weekly "Monday Drop" drove a ~90% sell-through on new releases and helped build a repeat-buyer cohort that made up roughly 30% of revenue by 2020. Expansion into the U.S., including the SoHo showroom "The Dome," shifted the revenue mix so U.S. sales exceeded 70% of total company revenue while inventory turnover ran about five times faster than traditional jewelers. Capital and Team Scaling Series A ($5M, 2018) and Series B ($23M, 2019) funded rapid scaling: headcount rose from ~20 to 100+ in 18 months, operationalizing product, marketing, and fulfillment functions. The funding supported a move into a major Toronto HQ and investments in real-time analytics to shorten production lead times. This capital foundation allowed Mejuri to balance growth runway with tight inventory economics. Product Strategy and Sell-Through The "Monday Drop" became Mejuri's signature launch mechanism, achieving ~90% sell-through on new SKUs and driving high-frequency engagement. Repeat buyers accounted for ~30% of revenue by 2020, demonstrating strong LTV potential. Real-time customer data allowed dynamic production scheduling, cutting markdowns and waste while keeping inventory turns ~5x faster than legacy jewelers.
